records.themeTitle: The place of distance can become the beginning of return
records.themeSummary: Abraham’s compromised surroundings and Israel’s exile can themselves awaken the wholehearted search for God; spiritual distance does not foreclose return.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ הָעִנְיָן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ: "לֶךְ לְךָ – לְאַתְקָנָא גַּרְמָךְ, לְאַתְקָנָא דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ וְכוּלֵי", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ, שֶׁאַף שֶׁנּוֹלַד מִתֶּרַח שֶׁהָיָה עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וּבְמָקוֹם שֶׁהָיוּ שְׁטוּפִין בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, לֹא יִפְחַד מִזֶּה, שֶׁאַדְּרַבָּה, מִזֶּה עַצְמוֹ יוּכַל לֵילֵךְ וּלְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָתוֹ. וְעַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם מִשָּׁם אֶת ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ וּמָצָאתָ וְגוֹמֵר", וְהוּא אַחַר שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וֶהֱפִיץ ה' אֶתְכֶם בָּעַמִּים וְגוֹמֵר", אַל יֵרַךְ לְבַבְכֶם לְהִתְיָאֵשׁ פֶּן חַס וְשָׁלוֹם תִּתְקַלְקְלוּ לְגַמְרֵי, כִּי אַדְּרַבָּה, מִשָּׁם דַּיְיקָא "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהַגָּלוּת יִגְרוֹם "כִּי תִדְרְשֶׁנּוּ בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל נַפְשֶׁךָ", וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם וּמָצָאתָ". וְכֵן אָמַר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ: "לֶךְ לְךָ" – לְאַתְקָנָא דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ, מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמוֹלַדְתְּךָ שֶׁנּוֹלַדְתָּ בְּמָקוֹם גָּרוּעַ וְשָׁפֵל, וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ שֶׁהָיָה תֶּרַח עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה – מִזֶּה עַצְמוֹ תּוּכַל לְתַקֵּן דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ.
records.originEnglish: The matter follows what is written in the holy Zohar: “Go for yourself—to put yourself right, to put your own level right,” and so forth. God was telling him that, although he was born to Terah, an idolater, in a place immersed in idolatry, he should not fear this. On the contrary, from that very situation he could advance and reach his level. This resembles “From there you shall seek the Lord your God, and you shall find Him,” which follows “The Lord will scatter you among the peoples.” Do not lose heart and despair, fearing that, God forbid, you will become completely corrupted. On the contrary, precisely “from there you shall seek”: the exile will bring about “when you seek Him with all your heart and all your soul,” and thereby “you shall seek and find.” So too, the blessed God told our father Abraham: “Go for yourself”—to put your own level right—“from your land and your birthplace,” having been born in a degraded, lowly place, “and from your father’s house,” Terah having been an idolater. From that very situation you can put your level right.
records.targetHebrew: אֵין לִיהוּדִי לְהִתְיָאֵשׁ מִשּׁוּם דָּבָר, בֵּין בְּעִנְיְנֵי הַגּוּף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב [בְּרָכוֹת י׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]: "אֲפִילּוּ חֶרֶב חַדָּה מֻנַּחַת עַל צַוָּארוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם אַל יִמְנַע עַצְמוֹ מִן הָרַחֲמִים", בֵּין בְּעִנְיְנֵי הַנֶּפֶשׁ, אֲפִילּוּ נִשְׁתַּקַּע לְמָקוֹם שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּקַּע וְחָטָא בְּדָבָר שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק א׳ רי״ט עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁאֵין תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת חַס וְחָלִילָה, אוֹ שֶׁתְּשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה, אוֹ שֶׁרוֹאֶה עַצְמוֹ מִשְׁתַּקֵּעַ וְהוֹלֵךְ בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אַל יִתְיָאֵשׁ בְּעַצְמוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לִפְרֹשׁ עוֹד, כִּי אֵין יֵאוּשׁ כְּלָל אֵצֶל אִישׁ יְהוּדִי, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לַעֲזֹר בְּכָל עִנְיָן. וְכָל בִּנְיַן אֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית הָיָה אַחַר הַיֵּאוּשׁ הַגָּמוּר, דְּ"אַבְרָהָם וְשָׂרָה זְקֵנִים", וּ"מִי מִלֵּל לְאַבְרָהָם הֵינִיקָה בָנִים שָׂרָה", שֶׁלֹּא עָלָה עַל דַּעַת אָדָם עוֹד לְהַאֲמִין זֶה וַאֲפִילּוּ אַחַר הַבְטָחַת הַמַּלְאָךְ;
records.targetEnglish: A Jew must not despair of anything: whether in bodily matters—as they said, “Even if a sharp sword rests upon a person’s neck, he must not refrain from seeking mercy”—or in matters of the soul. Even if he has sunk wherever he has sunk, and has sinned in a matter of which the Sages said that repentance does not avail, God forbid, or that repentance is difficult; or if he sees himself sinking ever further into the affairs of this world, he must not despair of himself and say that he can no longer break away. There is no despair at all for a Jew, and the blessed God can help in every matter. The entire building of the Israelite nation occurred after complete despair: “Abraham and Sarah were old,” and “Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?” No one any longer imagined believing this, even after the angel’s promise.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim gives the wider principle behind the reading of “from your land” and “from there you shall seek.” A condition that seems to make recovery impossible cannot establish that conclusion: Israel’s own beginning came after human expectation had failed. Peri Tzadik adds a more specific claim here: the experience of distance can itself generate the wholehearted seeking that brings a person back.

records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik gives the refusal to despair a precise scriptural mechanism. “From there” means that the place of exile itself can provoke wholehearted seeking. Abraham’s background therefore becomes material for his ascent, illuminating Divrei Soferim’s insistence that even deep spiritual entanglement does not close the possibility of return.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Hope remains when present expectation has failed
records.reverseThemeSummary: A Jew must not despair of bodily or spiritual recovery. Israel’s birth and Abraham’s rescue of Lot show why human expectation cannot rule out divine help.

records.themeTitle: Wealth calls for a renewed examination of the heart
records.themeSummary: Abraham experiences possessions as a spiritual burden and returns to prayer because success can introduce a new attachment to worldly desire.
records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁנִּכְנַס לְמִצְרַיִם, עֶרְוַת הָאָרֶץ, וְיָצָא מִשָּׁם עִם הַמַּתָּנוֹת, כְּתִיב: "וַיַּעַל אַבְרָם מִמִּצְרַיִם וְגוֹמֵר הַנֶּגְבָּה", וּכְתִיב: "וְאַבְרָם כָּבֵד מְאֹד בַּמִּקְנֶה וְגוֹמֵר", וּפֵירֵשׁ רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ זְצוּקַלְלָהּ"ה שֶׁהָיָה כָּבֵד עָלָיו וּלְמַשָּׂא כְּבֵדָה הַקִּנְיָנִים שֶׁקָּנָה, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁנִּתְיָירֵא פֶּן יִכָּנֵס בְּלִבּוֹ חֶמְדַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, דְּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי כְּתִיב "הַנֶּגְבָּה" שָׁם. וּכְתִיב: "וַיֵּלֶךְ וְגוֹמֵר אֶל מְקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְגוֹמֵר וַיִּקְרָא שָׁם אַבְרָם בְּשֵׁם ה'", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁהָלַךְ לְשָׁם לְהִתְפַּלֵּל עוֹד שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּנֵס הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע לְהַסְטִינוֹ.
records.originEnglish: Afterward, when he entered Egypt, “the nakedness of the land,” and left with the gifts, it is written, “Abram went up from Egypt ... toward the south,” and, “Abram was very heavy in livestock,” and so forth. Our holy master, of blessed memory, explained that the possessions he had acquired weighed upon him as a heavy burden, because he feared that desire for this world might enter his heart. This follows what we have explained, and is why “toward the south” is written there. It is also written, “He went ... to the place of the altar ... and there Abram called upon the name of the Lord.” This means that he went there to pray again that the evil inclination should not enter and lead him astray.

records.targetHebrew: "וַיִּבֶן שָׁם מִזְבֵּחַ לַה' וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם ה'". נִסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ הָיָה "לֶךְ לְךָ", הַיְינוּ עֲנִיּוּת וְצִמְצוּם, כִּי בָּזֶה צָרִיךְ הָאָדָם לְהִתְבָּרֵר תְּחִלָּה שֶׁלֹּא יִתְרַעֵם עַל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, אַךְ שֶׁיְּבַקֵּשׁ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלֹּא יָבֹא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְדִקְדּוּקֵי עֲנִיּוּת שֶׁמַּעֲבִירִין אֶת הָאָדָם עַל דַּעַת קוֹנוֹ. וְעִיקַּר דִּקְדּוּקֵי עֲנִיּוּת הַיְינוּ מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ שָׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וְרוֹצֶה בַּמּוֹתָרוֹת, וְעַל זֶה צָרִיךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְאַוֶּוה לַמּוֹתָרוֹת. כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיַעֲקֹב (בְּרֵאשִׁית כה, כז): "וְיַעֲקֹב אִישׁ תָּם", הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה שָׁלֵם בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מִבְּלִי שׁוּם תַּאֲוָה לַמּוֹתָרוֹת, רַק כְּפִי רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא יִתְבָּרַךְ כֵּן יְקַבֵּל בְּאַהֲבָה. וְכֵן הָיוּ תְּפִלּוֹת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּנִּסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה שָׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וְלֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ דִּקְדּוּקֵי עֲנִיּוּת; וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם ה'", הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָעֲנִיּוּת לֹא יַעֲבִירֶנּוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַל דַּעַת קוֹנוֹ. וְעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁחָזַר מִמִּצְרַיִם נֶאֱמַר: "וְאַבְרָם כָּבֵד מְאֹד", הַיְינוּ אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר בַּעֲנִיּוּת בְּבֵירוּר גָּמוּר בַּנִּסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן, נֶאֱמַר "כָּבֵד מְאֹד" לְשׁוֹן כְּבֵידוּת, שֶׁהָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ מִפְּנֵי הָעֲשִׁירוּת, כִּתְפִלַּת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (מִשְׁלֵי ל, ח): "רֵאשׁ וָעֹשֶׁר אַל תִּתֶּן לִי".
records.targetEnglish: “He built an altar there to the Lord, and called upon the name of the Lord.” Abraham our father’s first trial was “Go for yourself”: poverty and restriction. In this a person must first be tested and refined, so as not to complain against the blessed God, God forbid. Rather, he should ask God that he not fall into the grinding pressures of poverty that cause a person to transgress his Creator’s will. The essential pressure of poverty is when a person is not content with his portion and desires unnecessary extras; he must ask God not to desire them. Thus it is written of Jacob, “Jacob was a whole man”: he was whole within himself, without craving unnecessary things, accepting with love what accords with the Creator’s will. Such were Abraham our father’s prayers in the first trial: to be content with his portion and not suffer poverty’s grinding pressure. This is “he called upon the name of the Lord”: that poverty should not, God forbid, cause him to transgress his Creator’s will. Therefore, when he returned from Egypt it says, “Abram was very heavy.” After he had been completely refined through poverty in the first trial, “very heavy” expresses a burden: he feared for himself because of his wealth, like King Solomon’s prayer, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.”
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies the two-stage argument compressed into Rav Tzadok’s description of Abraham’s burden. Abraham first asks that deprivation not turn into resentment or craving; when that trial is complete, wealth requires a fresh examination. Peri Tzadik’s return to the altar is therefore an intelligible response to a new spiritual trial, even after earlier refinement.

records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik shows how the second trial affects Abraham’s movements: his wealth feels heavy because it may implant worldly desire, so he returns to the altar to pray again. This makes concrete Mei HaShiloach’s distinction between having endured poverty and still needing refinement in prosperity.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Wealth brings a fresh trial after poverty
records.reverseThemeSummary: Abraham first seeks contentment under deprivation. After that refinement, prosperity creates a new concern: possessions may burden the heart and require renewed prayer.

records.themeTitle: Every Jew inherits a real share in Torah
records.themeSummary: The blessing associated with Moses reaches the unlearned as well as the scholar: Torah belongs to the entire congregation of Jacob.
records.originHebrew: "וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה" – אַרְבַּע, נֶגֶד מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ, דִּכְתִיב: "וְזֹאת הַבְּרָכָה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרַךְ מֹשֶׁה וְגוֹמֵר", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁהוּא פָּעַל לְהוֹפִיעַ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "תּוֹרָה צִוָּה לָנוּ מֹשֶׁה מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב", וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): "'קְהִלַּת יַנַּאי' אֵין כְּתִיב כָּאן אֶלָּא 'קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב'", עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאַף עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ "בֵּית יַעֲקֹב", כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּדְרָשׁ בַּגְּמָרָא (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא לג עַמּוּד ב) "וּלְבֵית יַעֲקֹב", גַּם הֵם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה. וְזֶה הָיָה חֵלֶק הָעַם הָאָרֶץ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ לְרַבִּי יַנַּאי: "יְרוּשָׁתִי גַּבָּךְ", שֶׁאַף שֶׁלֹּא לָמַד, רַק פָּסוּק זֶה שֶׁשָּׁמַע וְהֵבִין בּוֹ שֶׁאַף עַם הָאָרֶץ יֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה.
records.originEnglish: “And be a blessing”—the fourth blessing corresponds to Moses our teacher, as it is written, “This is the blessing with which Moses blessed,” and so forth. He brought it about that words of Torah should shine within every individual Israelite, as it says, “Moses commanded us Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob.” The Midrash says: “It does not say ‘the congregation of Yannai,’ but ‘the congregation of Jacob’”; see there. Even the unlearned, who are called “the house of Jacob,” as the Talmud expounds in Bava Metzia on “and to the house of Jacob,” also have a share in Torah. This was the share of the unlearned man who said to Rabbi Yannai, “My inheritance is with you.” Though he had not studied, he had heard this one verse and understood from it that even an unlearned person has a share in Torah.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ הַמְשָׁכַת ״לֶחֶם מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם״ (שְׁמוֹת ט״ז:ד׳), וּכְמוֹ הַמָּן שֶׁנִּיתַּן לְיוֹצְאֵי מִצְרַיִם וְכֵן אִיתָא (מְכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח י״ז): ״לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא לְאוֹכְלֵי הַמָּן״ וַהֲרֵי הַתּוֹרָה נִיתְּנָה לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל: ״מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב״ (דְּבָרִים ל״ג:ד׳) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר אוֹתוֹ עַם הָאָרֶץ לְרַבִּי יַנַּאי: ״יְרוּשָׁתִי גַּבָּךְ״ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט:ג) וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּכוּלָּם אוֹכְלֵי מָן כִּי הָעוּגָה שֶׁהוֹצִיאוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם הָיָה בָּהּ טַעַם מָן (מְכִילְתָּא בֹּא י״ד) וְאִם כֵּן כָּל מַצָּה שֶׁהִיא עַל שֵׁם אוֹתָהּ עוּגָה, וַדַּאי גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ בָּהּ טַעַם מָן וּמִזֶּה הוּא הַמְשָׁכַת הַמָּזוֹן דְּכָל הַשָּׁנָה, דִּבְפֶסַח נִדּוֹנִין עַל הַתְּבוּאָה, כְּמָה שֶׁכָּתוּב (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ט״ז עַמּוּד א׳) דְּעַל יְדֵי לֶחֶם עוֹנִי זֶה שֶׁאוֹכְלִין בְּמִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּמַכִּירִין עָנְיָם וְשִׁפְלוּתָם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם רַק מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן עַל יְדֵי זֶה מַמְשִׁיכִין הַשְׁפָּעָתוֹ וּנְתִינָתוֹ: ״נֹתֵן לֶחֶם לְכָל בָּשָׂר [כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ]״ (תְּהִלִּים קל״ו:כ״ה) וְנִמְצָא כָּל הַלֶּחֶם טַעַם מָן: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ אַחַר כָּךְ: ״הוֹדוּ לְאֵל הַשָּׁמַיִם כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ״ (תְּהִלִּים קל״ו:כ״ו) הַיְינוּ דְּלֶחֶם זֶה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מִן הָאָרֶץ, נַעֲשָׂה בִּקְדֻשַּׁת ״לֶחֶם מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם״ מֵאַחַר שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן
records.targetEnglish: This is the drawing down of “bread from heaven,” like the manna given to those who left Egypt. So it is taught: “The Torah was given only to those who ate the manna.” Yet the Torah was given to all Israel, “an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob,” as that unlearned man said to Rabbi Yannai, “My inheritance is with you.” Necessarily, then, they are all eaters of manna. For the cake they brought out of Egypt had the taste of manna. Consequently, every matzah that commemorates that cake certainly also has the taste of manna. From this comes the nourishment of the entire year, for on Passover judgment is passed concerning grain. Through this bread of poverty, eaten at God’s command, they recognize their poverty and lowliness: they have only what the blessed God gives. Thereby they draw down His bounty and gift, “Who gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness is forever.” All bread is thus found to have the taste of manna. This explains the next verse, “Give thanks to the God of heaven, for His kindness is forever”: although this bread comes from the earth, it takes on the holiness of bread from heaven when one recognizes that the blessed God is its giver.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz uses the same unlearned man’s claim as a premise with consequences. If Torah is truly everyone’s inheritance, the nourishment associated with receiving it must also reach everyone. Its explanation of earthly bread becoming “manna” through recognizing the Giver extends the universal blessing in Peri Tzadik into ordinary life.

records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, since words of Torah have been apportioned to the entire congregation of Jacob, even to the lowliest soul, someone who is truly a Torah scholar must recognize, through the outward garment of proper conduct that he sees in an unlearned person, the depth and preciousness of the point of Torah within him. This is why the man seized him and said, “My inheritance is with you. It does not say ‘the congregation of Yannai,’ but ‘the congregation of Jacob.’” God has apportioned words of Torah to all the souls of Israel, so that even the lowliest Israelite cannot, God forbid, be wholly without Torah. In the point of Torah found in each individual, that person is truly distinguished and raised above all Israel. He therefore seized Rabbi Yannai and said, “My inheritance is with you”: although I myself do not recognize the words of Torah in the depth of my heart, because I am unlearned, you, Rabbi Yannai, are a Torah scholar. From the proper conduct I possess, you should have discerned and demonstrated the preciousness of the point of Torah within me, from which all that proper conduct branches out. These truthful words awakened Rabbi Yannai. He immediately acknowledged them and regretted what he had said: “All this proper conduct is with you, and I called you a dog!”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why the man’s “inheritance” matters even when he cannot demonstrate conventional Torah learning. His proper conduct expresses a distinctive inward point of Torah, and the scholar has a responsibility to recognize it. This develops Rav Tzadok’s brief assertion that the unlearned also receive Moses’ blessing into an account of what their share can look like and how a teacher should respond.

This provides the larger setting for Sod Yesharim’s demand that a scholar recognize an individual point of Torah even when it appears through conduct rather than learned speech.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Recognizing the Torah inheritance within another person
records.reverseThemeSummary: God gives every Israelite a distinctive point of Torah. The scholar must recognize it even when an unlearned person expresses it through proper conduct rather than conventional learning.

records.themeTitle: Sin can obscure the root of the heart without severing it
records.themeSummary: The myrtle remains a myrtle among thorns: Israel’s inward bond to God makes repentance and the restoration of joy possible even after sin.
records.originHebrew: דְּאָסָא מָצִינוּ (מְגִילָּה יג עַמּוּד א): "הַצַּדִּיקִים שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ הֲדַסִּים", וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים". וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ (צג עַמּוּד א): "וְהָא כַּמָּה חַיָּיבִין אִית בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כַּמָּה חַטָּאִין וְכַמָּה רְשִׁיעִין וְכוּלֵי, אֶלָּא וְכוּלֵי, דִּמְקָרְבִין בְּנַיְיהוּ לִתְמַנְיָא יוֹמִין לְקָרְבָּנָא, וְכַד אִתְגְּזַרוּ וְכוּלֵי אִקְרוּן צַדִּיקִים וְכוּלֵי", וְהַיְינוּ עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד עַמּוּד א) עַל הַפָּסוּק "חָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל": "אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא – יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא; אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא: הַיְינוּ דְּאָמְרֵי אִינָשֵׁי: אָסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי חִילְפֵי, אָסָא שְׁמֵיהּ וְאָסָא קָרוּ לֵיהּ". וְהוּא, שֶׁכֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּימּוֹל הַתִּינוֹק לִשְׁמוֹנָה שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ וְנַעֲשָׂה עַל יְדֵי כֵן יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְזֶה מוֹרֶה שֶׁקָּשׁוּר בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, וְכָל מַה שֶּׁעוֹבֵר עָלָיו, בֶּאֱמֶת: "רְצוֹנֵנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ, וּמִי מְעַכֵּב? שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה וְכוּלֵי", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת יז עַמּוּד א).
records.originEnglish: Concerning myrtle, we find: “The righteous are called myrtles.” All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says, “Your people are all righteous.” The holy Zohar in this portion asks: “But how many guilty people there are in Israel, how many sinners and how many wicked people!” It answers that they bring their children at eight days old as an offering, and when they are circumcised they are called righteous. This accords with what the Talmud says about “Israel has sinned”: “Even though he has sinned, he is still Israel.” Rabbi Abba said: This is what people say: “A myrtle standing among the thorn bushes is named a myrtle, and a myrtle they call it.” Since the infant is circumcised at eight days without his conscious choice and thereby becomes Israel, this indicates that he is bound at his root to the blessed God, in the beginning of divine thought. Whatever he undergoes, the truth is: “Our will is to do Your will; what prevents us? The leaven in the dough,” and so forth, as written in Berakhot.

records.targetEnglish: Likewise, someone who is wicked in actual deed is so only through the inclination; it does not come from his heart. records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz distinguishes the person’s actual sinful deed from the enduring depth of the heart, and identifies remorse as an expression of that hidden good. records.themeTitle: Wine reveals what already fills the heart
records.themeSummary: Joseph’s meal tests an inward bond: the secret that emerges when ordinary composure recedes depends on what has taken root within the person.

On Shabbat the will of Atika, the Ancient One, is revealed: by day is the meal of Atika, and at the Friday-night meal the Holy Ancient One comes to dine with her [the Shekhinah]. Knowledge, which is the inwardness of the supernal crown, is revealed, and for this reason drinking is permitted then. Joseph’s intention in giving them wine was to learn the depths of their hearts: were they bound to the root? records.targetEnglish: “In his cup” corresponds to “with all your heart,” as it is written, “Wine and new wine take away the heart.” The heart’s test comes when it is unsettled. If its entire space is already truly filled, from one side to the other, with love of the blessed God, then even when wine enters, the secret of the Lord hidden within it comes out. The whole matter of trials occurs through taking away the heart [its settled awareness], as I heard concerning Amaziah, and likewise concerning Hezekiah, of whom it says, “God left him, to test him.” Therefore Abraham our father, who corresponds to “with all your heart,” underwent trials. His essential quality is love of the blessed God, “with all your heart,” as they said: “The Merciful One desires the heart.”
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the test that Rav Tzadok attributes to Joseph. Wine reduces settled awareness; what then emerges discloses the heart’s existing content. The qualification “if its entire space is already filled” is essential: it clarifies why Peri Tzadik first establishes the meal’s Shabbat holiness and the brothers’ attachment to the root before discussing intoxication.

records.reverseThemeTitle: The cup as a test of love that fills the heart
records.reverseThemeSummary: The cup, purse, and anger test the dimensions of love expressed in “all your heart, all your soul, and all your might.” What emerges through wine depends on the love already filling the heart.

records.targetEnglish: This is what the blessed God said to Abraham: “Go for yourself.” Tanchuma expounds: “Move yourself from place to place,” giving the parable of a flask of balsam. Through his displacement the inwardness of his heart will become known, and the good depths of his heart will come into action. He is to conceal the deficiency at the root, so that it does not spread outward and will consequently perish. A person reaches this through his service of the blessed God by entering the actions and affairs of this world; through this, what a person is becomes recognizable. Thus the Talmud says: “A person is recognized in three things: his cup, his purse, and his anger.” It does not give as a sign for recognizing someone the time when he stands in the synagogue wrapped in a mitzvah tallit and crowned with tefillin, implying that this provides no proof. The principal recognition comes when he enters the concealments of worldly affairs, dealing with people in the markets and streets. Then one can recognize a person’s preciousness: what lies in the depths of his heart.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov places the cup among situations that expose inward character when outward religious presentation cannot establish it. Its reading of Abraham’s journeys makes such exposure part of bringing hidden goodness into action. This helps explain Joseph’s concern with the brothers’ “depths of the heart”: the meal reveals the inner bond that the visible act of drinking alone cannot establish.

records.themeTitle: Holy intention requires a form that can actually sanctify desire
records.themeSummary: Noah’s wish to repair the heart does not make every pleasure an instrument of repair; the ois distinguishes mitzvah, Torah need, and an assumed spiritual benefit.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה הָעִנְיָן בְּנֹחַ גַּם כֵּן: אַחַר שֶׁהוּתַּר לוֹ הַבָּשָׂר כְּדֵי שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַבָּשָׂר יִזְכֶּה לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשַׂמְּחוֹ, הָיָה נֹחַ סָבוּר שֶׁאַף הַיַּיִן נִצְרָךְ לוֹ לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וְלִזְכּוֹת לְשִׂמְחָה, וְאֵין רְאָיָה מֵאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל; וְזֶה הָיָה טַעֲמוֹ שֶׁנָּטַע כֶּרֶם. אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת, הַיַּיִן הַמְיַישֵּׁר הַלֵּב הוּא רַק יַיִן דְּקִדּוּשׁ שֶׁהוּא יַיִן מִצְוָה, אוֹ מִי שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ לוֹ הַיַּיִן לְיִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת לְתוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג, קכד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): "חַכִּימִין דְּדַמְיָין לְשַׁבַּתּוֹת וְכוּלֵי", וְכָל אֲכִילָתָן בִּקְדוּשָׁה, כַּאֲכִילַת שַׁבָּתוֹת וְיוֹם טוֹב שֶׁכָּל אֲכִילָתָן לְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים לְתוֹרָה; וְלָהֶם נִצְרָךְ הַיַּיִן כְּמוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁאָדָם קוֹבֵעַ סְעוּדָתוֹ עַל הַיַּיִן.
records.originEnglish: This also explains Noah’s case. After meat was permitted to him, so that through it he could set his heart straight and gladden it, Noah thought that wine was likewise needed to set the heart straight and attain joy. Adam’s situation before the damage, he thought, provided no proof against this. That was his reason for planting a vineyard. In truth, however, the wine that sets the heart straight is only the wine of Kiddush, which is wine used for a mitzvah, or wine needed by someone for the mental composure necessary for Torah. As the holy Zohar says, “Sages who resemble Sabbaths”: all their eating is in holiness, like eating on Shabbat and festivals, for all their eating sustains life for Torah. For them wine is needed as it is on Shabbat, when a person establishes his meal over wine.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרָכוֹת נד.: "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ" – בִּשְׁנֵי יְצָרֶיךָ: בְּיֵצֶר טוֹב הוּא בְּאִתְכַּפְיָא וּמִלְחָמָה, וּבְיֵצֶר רָע הוּא אַחַר שֶׁנִּצְּחוֹ, מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּכֹחוֹתָיו לְטוֹב. וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת יוֹסֵף וְדָוִד: יוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק הָיָה בְּנִצּוּחַ וְהַגְדָּרָה מִתַּאֲוָה; וְדָוִד, אַדְּרַבָּה, כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה הָיָה בַּעַל תַּאֲוָה, רַק שֶׁהָיוּ אוֹתָם מַצָּעוֹת בְּהֶיתֵּר וּבִקְדוּשָּׁה, שֶׁהוּא קָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ "חָסִיד", לְפִי שֶׁמְּלוּכָה הוּא נִצּוּחַ, וּמֶלֶךְ אֵינוֹ רַק אֶחָד, וְאֵין הַכֹּל מְלָכִים רַק בְּנֵי מְלָכִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שַׁבָּת סז. וְהָבֵן; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן צַדִּיק – יְסוֹד עוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ. וְזֶהוּ אוֹת בְּרִית דְּקֶשֶׁת לְנֹחַ, כַּיָּדוּעַ שֶׁהוּא רוֹמֵז לְמִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף: "וַתֵּשֶׁב בְּאֵיתָן קַשְׁתּוֹ" בְּרֵאשִׁית מט, כד, שֶׁהוּא הַהַגְדָּרָה בְּהִיפּוּךְ כְּמַדְרֵגַת נֹחַ.
records.targetEnglish: This is what they said in Berakhot: “With all your heart”—with both your inclinations. With the good inclination, service takes the form of subduing and fighting; with the evil inclination, after one has conquered it, one uses its powers for good. This is the distinction between the levels of Joseph and David. Joseph the righteous served through conquest and placing bounds against desire. David, by contrast, appeared to be a man of desire, but those couches [previously prepared for sin] were used permissibly and in holiness. He called himself “pious,” because kingship means conquest. There is only one king, and not everyone is a king: they are children of kings, as our Sages said in Shabbat; understand this. The righteous one, by contrast, is the foundation of the entire world. This is the sign of the rainbow covenant given to Noah. As is known, it alludes to Joseph’s quality: “His bow remained firm.” This is the setting of a boundary through opposition, corresponding to Noah’s level.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah distinguishes resisting desire from employing its powers after conquest, and explicitly associates Noah with the former task of setting boundaries. This clarifies the limit in Peri Tzadik: Noah cannot infer that wine will sanctify his heart merely because bodily nourishment can serve a holy purpose. The relevant spiritual capacity and the concrete form of service still matter.

records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik explains Noah’s vineyard as an attempted repair rather than a simple wish for pleasure, but shows why its spiritual premise was insufficient. Its distinction between wine used for a mitzvah or Torah and Noah’s assumption illustrates Kometz HaMinchah’s rule that using desire for holiness belongs to a level attained after conquest.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Conquering desire before using its powers for holiness
records.reverseThemeSummary: Opposition and restraint belong to the struggle with desire; employing its powers for good follows conquest. Noah and the rainbow illustrate the work of setting a boundary.

records.targetEnglish: The Talmud states: Rabbi Levi bar Hama said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, “A person should always stir the good inclination against the evil inclination,” as it says, “Tremble and do not sin.” If he conquers it, well and good; if not, he should engage in Torah, as it says, “Speak in your hearts.” If he conquers it, well and good; if not, he should recite the Shema, as it says, “Upon your beds.” If he conquers it, well and good; if not, he should remind himself of the day of death, as it says, “And be still. Selah.” Rabbi Levi bar Hama says “always” because in every situation a person undergoes, even in matters of great spiritual attainments, he must continually discern and test whether it comes from the blessed God or whether, God forbid, some trace and dross of something else is present. Especially when an occasion of joy comes to a person, it requires still greater examination. Therefore four levels of counsel are mentioned here, showing how to discern and reach the depth of truth. Afterward, when he knows clearly that it comes from God, he can give it expression, knowing that it is a mitzvah or the joy of a mitzvah.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies a discipline of examination for precisely the inference that fails in Noah’s vineyard: even an apparently elevated impulse and a desire for joy must be tested before being identified as a mitzvah. Its context is Jacob’s joy on hearing that Joseph lives. The conceptual link is the need to establish the holiness of joy, rather than assuming it from the strength or spiritual language of the desire.

records.themeTitle: Blessing after eating directs the food’s strength toward holiness
records.themeSummary: Food strengthens the heart in one direction or the other. Recognizing and thanking the Giver determines how its vitality is received.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן אַחַר שֶׁסּוֹעֵד, דְּאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יב עַמּוּד ב): "אַחַר שֶׁאוֹכֵל וְשׁוֹתֶה אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא לֵב אֶחָד", וְלֹא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ אֵיזֶה לֵב אֶחָד, שֶׁמִּקּוֹדֶם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁנֵי לְבָבוֹת, הַיְינוּ יֵצֶר טוֹב וְיֵצֶר רָע, וּלְאַחַר שֶׁאָכַל וְשָׁתָה, אִם הָיְתָה אֲכִילָתוֹ בִּקְדוּשָׁה, יֵשׁ לוֹ רַק לֵב אֶחָד לַאֲבִיהוּ שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָׁה מְתַקֵּן הַפְּגָם שֶׁהָיָה בָּאֲכִילָה; וְאִם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם הָאֲכִילָה לְשֵׁם תַּאֲוָה, אָז עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה גּוֹרֵם קִטְרוּג יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאֵין יֵצֶר הָרָע שׁוֹלֵט אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ בְּסִפְרֵי מִכַּמָּה פְסוּקִים. וְעַל יְדֵי בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ אַחַר אֲכִילָתוֹ פּוֹעֵל שֶׁלֹּא יַזִּיק אֲכִילָתוֹ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁמַּכִּיר כֹּחַ הַנּוֹתֵן, וּכְשֶׁבָּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ גוֹרֵם קִטְרוּג יֵצֶר הָרָע. וְכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נג עַמּוּד ב): "'וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם' – אֵלּוּ מַיִם רִאשׁוֹנִים, 'וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים' – אֵלּוּ מַיִם אַחֲרוֹנִים וְכוּלֵי", וְכָל זֶה עֵצָה שֶׁתִּהְיֶה הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָׁה.
records.originEnglish: Likewise after a meal: the Talmud says, “After a person eats and drinks, he has only one heart.” It does not specify which one heart. Beforehand he has two hearts, the good inclination and the evil inclination. After he eats and drinks, if his eating was in holiness, he has only one heart toward his Father in heaven, for through holy eating he repairs the damage that came through eating. But if, God forbid, his eating is for the sake of desire, his eating gives rise to the evil inclination’s accusation; the evil inclination gains control through eating and drinking, as the Sifrei derives from several verses. Through the Grace after Meals that he recites after eating, he brings it about that his eating does no harm, because he recognizes the power of the Giver. When it comes from the blessed God, it does not give rise to the evil inclination’s accusation. So they expounded: “Sanctify yourselves”—the first washing of the hands; “and you shall be holy”—the final washing, and so forth. All this is counsel that eating should take place in holiness.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה טַעַם מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּעֵירוּבִין [נ״ד עַמּוּד א׳]: "חֲטֹף וֶאֱכוֹל וְכוּלֵי, כְּהִלּוּלָא דָּמְיָא": פֵּרוּשׁ, הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא יִחוּד חָתָן וְכַלָּה, הַיְינוּ קַבָּלַת הָאָדָם הַשֶּׁפַע מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, זֶהוּ רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא עֵסֶק הָאָדָם בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא וְהַחֵשֶׁק, וּמְקַבֵּל הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא וְהַמִּלּוּי דְּמַיִּין דּוּכְרִין לְעֻמָּתוֹ, וְהוּא הַחֲתֻנָּה; וְ"אַגְרָא דְּבֵי הִלּוּלָא — מִילֵּי", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק: "אָדָם לְעָמָל יוּלָּד" — לַעֲמַל פֶּה בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה הֵם מְשַׂמְּחִים חָתָן וְכַלָּה, וּמְעוֹרְרִים מַיִּין נוּקְבִין בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא בִּתְפִלָּה וּמַיִּין דּוּכְרִין דִּלְעֵילָא בַּתּוֹרָה; וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יְיַחֵד יִחוּדִים גַּם כֵּן בַּאֲכִילָתוֹ, הַיְינוּ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג הַנֹּכַח דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא הַמְחַיֶּה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא "חֲטֹף וֶאֱכוֹל", שֶׁחוֹטֵף וְטוֹרֵף אוֹתָם הָעֲשׁוּקִים לְתוֹךְ הַקְּדוּשָּׁה. וּלְכָךְ מַסֶּכֶת נָזִיר שֶׁעִנְיָנָהּ הַגְדָּרַת הַתַּאֲווֹת מְסַיֶּמֶת: "חֲטֹף וּבָרֵיךְ", כִּי לִירֵאָיו הַמֻּגְדָּרִים בְּתַאֲווֹת נִתַּן הַחֲטִיפָה, וְעַל כֵּן "וּבָרֵיךְ", דְּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן הַהוֹדָאָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּשֶׁהוּא שָׂבֵעַ — זֶהוּ גְּמַר הַחֲטִיפָה.
records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of what is written in Eruvin: “Snatch and eat ... for it resembles a wedding feast.” This world is the union of groom and bride: a person’s receiving bounty from the blessed God. This occurs only in this world, where a person’s work involves awakening from below and desire, and he receives in response an awakening from above and the fulfillment of the masculine waters. This is the wedding. “The reward of a wedding feast is words”: as the Sages said in the chapter Helek, “Man is born to toil”—the toil of the mouth in Torah and prayer. Through this they gladden groom and bride, arousing feminine waters through prayer’s awakening from below and masculine waters from above through Torah. Thereby a person also effects unifications in eating: he apprehends the presence of the blessed God as the One who gives life. Through this he “snatches and eats,” seizing those oppressed sparks into holiness. Therefore tractate Nazir, whose concern is setting bounds to desires, ends with “Snatch and bless.” Those who fear God and set bounds to their desires are given this power of seizing. Hence “and bless”: the Grace after Meals, thanking the blessed God when one is satisfied, completes the act of seizing.
records.explanation: Et HaOchel explains the positive action accomplished by the recognition of the Giver in Peri Tzadik. Torah, prayer, and thanksgiving receive nourishment as God’s life-giving bounty and bring its vitality into holiness; the blessing after satisfaction completes that movement. This gives content to Rav Tzadok’s claim that eating can leave the person with one heart directed toward God.

Recognition of the Giver prevents nourishment from feeding the evil inclination. This clarifies Et HaOchel’s description of Grace after Meals as completing the rescue of the food’s vitality into holiness.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Thanksgiving completes the elevation of nourishment
records.reverseThemeSummary: Eating in measured holiness directs food’s vitality toward the good inclination. Torah, prayer, and thanksgiving bring that vitality to its source, with Grace after Meals completing the movement.
